fields.meta_title: Ebook Landing Page: Examples and Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an ebook landing page that emails the book on request or sells it through Stripe, with four examples followed past the form.
fields.h1: Build an Ebook Landing Page That Delivers Every Copy
fields.hero_description: Create an ebook landing page that emails the book to each reader and records every request in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Happens After the Download Button
fields.features_subheading: Readers judge the cover. Whether the ebook pays off is decided once the form goes in.
fields.feature_1:
Delivery by email, not by redirect

The form emails a download link to the address the visitor typed. Visitors who want the book give an address they read, because a mistyped or invented one never receives it.
fields.feature_2:
The cover and chapter list beside the form

Upload the cover and the table of contents, and Emergent places both next to the form. Visitors see what the book covers before they sign up, and phones show the cover first.
fields.feature_3:
Fields that decide the follow-up

Company size or role belongs on the form only when it changes what happens next. Emergent adds the field and writes each answer into the reader's row, where a routing rule reads it.
fields.feature_4:
A reader table with the source attached

Every request becomes a row with the reader's email, the title asked for, the time, and the utm_source of the link that brought them. Rows sync to HubSpot or any CRM with an API.
fields.feature_5:
Checkout for the ebooks you sell

Stripe takes the payment, and the download link appears only after Stripe confirms it. Paid orders land in the same table as free requests, with the amount and the buyer's email.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take elsewhere

Export the page and its reader table to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A custom domain on Emergent uses credits; the exported code also runs on any server you choose.

fields.tab_content_1:
Readers from large companies go to sales first

Ledgerline gates its month-end close playbook behind a work email and company size. When the company has 200 or more employees, account executive Dana Ortiz gets a direct message in Slack with the name and headcount. Companies under 200 employees get the playbook, then a follow-up four days later.
fields.tab_content_2:
Chapter one now, the store links on release day

Novelist Nadia Brooks gives away chapter one of Tidewater Hours to anyone who leaves an address, and it lands in their inbox moments later. By the week before release, 1,240 readers had signed up. At 9 AM on release day, each of them gets a single email carrying the store links.
fields.tab_content_3:
Download link released after the payment clears

For $24, Studio Margin sells its ebook on pricing design work through Stripe Checkout. Once Stripe reports the payment, the buyer lands on a page with the download button, and the same link arrives by email. The link expires after 7 days, and a buyer who misses it can request a fresh one from the order page.
fields.tab_content_4:
Each reader tagged by the guides they picked

Six growing guides sit on one page at Fernhill Garden Supply, and visitors choose up to three before entering an address. Every pick becomes a tag on the subscriber's row. Tomatoes leads this month with 318 requests, and the spring note about tomatoes goes only to those 318 people.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Ebook Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to an ebook landing page that delivers the book by email and shows which readers become customers.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Lead with the problem the book solves
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Show the cover and what is inside
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Cut every field nobody acts on
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write the headline around the reader's problem, such as closing the books in five days, not around the ebook's title. The title already sits on the cover image, and the headline has a different job: telling the right visitor to keep reading.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put the cover next to the form and list the chapters under it, with a page count. A visitor deciding whether an ebook deserves an email address wants to see that it answers their exact question before scrolling to the button.
fields.howto_step_3_des: An email address is enough to deliver the book. Company size earns a place when sales follows up on large accounts, and job role earns one when the next message changes by role. Every other field is work for the reader with nothing in return.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Email the download link instead of opening the file on the next screen. The address has to work for the book to arrive, and the reader can find the link in their inbox a week later. Say on the confirmation screen where the link was sent.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Record where each reader came from
fields.howto_step_5_des: Add utm_source and utm_campaign to the links in your posts and ads, then save both values with each request. The reader table then shows which channel brings people who later buy, not only which channel brings the most requests.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Decide what follows the book before the page goes live. A note three days later that points to the most useful chapter gets the ebook opened. A demo request the next morning asks for more than the reader has offered so far.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Judge the page by what follows
fields.howto_step_7_des: Count requests against visits to the page, then follow the rows: how many people booked a call or bought within 90 days. An ebook that draws fewer requests but more buyers is the one to promote in the next campaign.

plan.angle: The top 10 is design galleries (Dribbble, Pinterest, Behance, Envato), example roundups from page builders (Leadpages, MailerLite, Unbounce, SeedProd) and one template listing (Landingi). All of them judge an ebook page by its cover and headline and stop at the button. This page defines the term for the AI Overview, then follows four ebook pages past the form: a B2B guide whose large-company readers reach an account executive in Slack, a novelist's free first chapter feeding a release-day email, a paid ebook sold through Stripe with the link released after payment, and a garden retailer's six-guide library that tags each reader by pick. The how-to covers delivery by email, field choice and source tracking with UTM parameters.
tab_stories: Ledgerline's month-end close playbook asks for a work email and company size, and when the company has 200 or more employees the account executive Dana Ortiz gets a Slack direct message while smaller companies get a follow-up email.
Novelist Nadia Brooks sends chapter one of Tidewater Hours to anyone who enters an email, and the 1,240 readers on that list get one email with the store links at 9 AM on release day.
Studio Margin sells a $24 ebook on pricing design work through Stripe Checkout, releases the download link only after Stripe confirms payment, and lets the link expire after 7 days.
Fernhill Garden Supply offers six growing guides on one page, visitors pick up to three, every pick becomes a tag, and the spring note about tomatoes goes only to the 318 people who chose that guide.

scope.evidence: H1 "Build an Ebook Landing Page That Delivers Every Copy"; hero "Create an ebook landing page that emails the book to each reader and records every request in a database you own." (115 chars, leads with the verb); how-to description one sentence, 113 chars.

intent.evidence: Top 10 is example galleries and roundups; meta promises "four examples followed past the form" and the tabs deliver four worked ebook pages (B2B gated, sample chapter, paid, library), plus a 7-step how-to and an examples/template/design FAQ.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: "utm_source and utm_campaign", "Stripe Checkout", "company size", "table of contents"; table generated from the library with Unbounce and Landingi/Leadpages from the top 10.

openers.evidence: Body paragraphs open on full sentences ("The form emails a download link...", "Ledgerline gates its month-end close playbook..."); three FAQ fragment openers recorded as a note.

craft.evidence: QC Q2/Q5/Q7 clean; sentences carry one idea ("The link expires after 7 days, and a buyer who misses it can request a fresh one from the order page.").

voice.evidence: Concrete, unglamorous detail: "a follow-up four days later", "1,240 readers", "318 requests"; no AI tells (QC A1 clean). Shared sibling formulas recorded as a note.

truth.evidence: claims_used all in capabilities.json (custom-domain "uses credits", code-export "on paid plans"); Stripe, Slack, HubSpot, UTM and 7-day link facts each have a domain_sources entry; 318+264+187+152+96+71=1,088 in tab 4.

distinct.evidence: No sibling primary (lead magnet, whitepaper, case study landing page) in any heading; tab stories unique to ebooks (chapter one, paid download, guide library).

faq.evidence: Exactly 10 on-topic questions, no brands or formats in questions; hub link in item 2, two sibling links (thank-you-page, webinar-landing-page); all 7 secondaries placed once; F9 moat lines in items 4 and 7.

images.evidence: Brief matches copy: tab 1 "To Dana Ortiz" / "Slack direct message" / "Under 200 employees: follow-up in 4 days"; tab 2 "1,240" and "9 AM, release day"; tab 3 "$24.00" and "In 7 days"; tab 4 "Tomatoes, 318 people". One hero per tab; share image reads cleanly.
